title: Pulmonary embolism: pretest probability, D-dimer, and when to image

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2019 ESC pulmonary embolism guideline and ACP guidance on evaluation. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which items score three points in the Wells score for pulmonary embolism?
a: Clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis
Pulmonary embolism is the most likely diagnosis
questions.why: Heart rate, immobilisation or surgery, and previous thromboembolism score 1.5; haemoptysis and cancer score 1. Over 4 is 'likely' and goes straight to imaging.

questions.q: When is a D-dimer the right test?
questions.a: When the pretest probability is low or intermediate
d: In every patient with chest pain
questions.why: A high-probability patient goes to imaging regardless of the D-dimer; a negative result there is not safe. A normal D-dimer with low probability ends the work-up.

questions.q: How is the D-dimer cutoff adjusted for a 70-year-old?
questions.why: The age-adjusted cutoff applies over 50 and roughly doubles the number of older patients who can be spared imaging without missing emboli.

questions.q: The PERC rule allows a low-probability patient to skip all testing when which of these are absent?
questions.why: Also absent: haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling, and surgery or trauma in the past four weeks. All eight must be negative, and the clinician's gestalt must already be low.

questions.q: What is the first-line imaging test for suspected pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: A ventilation-perfusion scan is used when contrast is contraindicated. Echocardiography is for the unstable patient too sick to leave the room, where right ventricular strain supports the diagnosis.

questions.q: A pregnant woman has suspected pulmonary embolism. What is a reasonable first imaging step?
questions.a: Compression ultrasound of the legs; if negative, proceed to lung imaging
questions.why: A leg thrombosis confirms the diagnosis without radiation. Both CT angiography and a perfusion scan are acceptable after that; the fetal dose from either is small.

questions.q: Pulmonary embolism is likely and the CT will take an hour. What is done now?
questions.a: Start anticoagulation while awaiting the scan
questions.why: For intermediate or high probability, the risk of delay outweighs the risk of a few hours of anticoagulation in a patient who turns out not to have an embolus.

questions.q: A systolic blood pressure below what, sustained for 15 minutes, defines high-risk pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: Or a drop of 40 mm Hg from baseline, or the need for vasopressors. These patients get systemic thrombolysis unless it is contraindicated.

questions.q: A normotensive patient has right ventricular strain on CT and a raised troponin. What is the treatment?
questions.a: Anticoagulation with close monitoring; thrombolysis only if they deteriorate
questions.why: Routine thrombolysis in this intermediate-high risk group reduced decompensation but raised major bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, so it is held in reserve.

questions.q: Which are absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis?
questions.why: Age and pregnancy are relative contraindications. In a patient with an absolute contraindication and shock, catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy is the route.

questions.q: Which score identifies a patient with pulmonary embolism who can be treated at home?
questions.a: The simplified PESI, at a score of zero
questions.why: Its items are age over 80, cancer, cardiopulmonary disease, heart rate 110 or more, systolic under 100, and saturation under 90%. Any one point means admission.

questions.q: A CT shows a single subsegmental embolus, leg ultrasound is negative, and the patient is well with no cancer. Which option is reasonable?
d: Six months of anticoagulation is mandatory
questions.why: Isolated subsegmental findings are often false positives. With a negative leg scan and no risk factors, surveillance is accepted; anticoagulation is given if there is cancer, immobility, or symptoms.
